headline: Oklahoma Ranchers Use Fire to Protect Grasslands and Stop Wildfires
meta_description: Father-son ranchers Chuck and Seth Coffey use carefully controlled burns to restore prairie health and prevent catastrophic wildfires across Oklahoma's grassla…
summary_short: Great Plains ranchers are deliberately burning their land in winter to revitalize prairies, control invasive trees, and stop dangerous wildfires before they start.
body:
Across southern Oklahoma's Arbuckle Mountains, controlled flames move through prairie grass in what looks like disaster but is actually restoration. Father-son ranchers Chuck and Seth Coffey of the Double C Cattle Company have joined a growing movement of Great Plains landowners who use prescribed burns—strategically timed, carefully managed fires—to keep their grasslands healthy and productive. The Coffeys and their neighbors burned close to 22,000 acres this year, clearing land of dense vegetation before dangerous spring winds arrive. By burning in late winter, they eliminate fuel that could feed catastrophic wildfires later in the season, giving them control over when and how fire moves across their landscape.

The real problem these ranchers are solving runs deeper than wildfire prevention. Over two centuries of fire suppression, eastern red cedar trees have invaded hundreds of thousands of acres of historically open prairie. These fast-growing trees drain aquifers, produce nothing for livestock to eat, and burn hotter than grass when wildfires arrive. Chuck Coffey inherited portions of the ranch with 60 percent tree canopy coverage; through prescribed burns combined with cutting and herbicide spraying, tree cover on that land now stands at just 17 percent. His goal: not a single cedar tree remaining.

What started as one family's mission has become a community solution. The Coffeys helped launch the Arbuckle Rangeland Restoration Association so neighboring ranchers could share resources and coordinate burns across larger areas. Similar burn associations are spreading across the Great Plains, from Oklahoma to Nebraska's Sandhills—the most intact temperate grassland left on Earth. Fire departments have become unexpected allies, using already-burned areas on ranches as safe bases to fight remaining wildfires. For ranchers like Barb Cooksley in Nebraska, the message is simple: "We burn as neighbors. We're all looking for a solution to the same problem."
quick_facts: Double C Cattle Company spans roughly 30,000 contiguous acres in southern Oklahoma
Tree canopy cover reduced from 60% to 17% through prescribed burns and restoration
The Coffeys burned close to 22,000 acres in one year with neighbors combined
Nebraska Sandhills region is the most intact temperate grassland left on Earth
